title: Working capital management
log: 2026-10-29T12:22:32Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: No point in the bank teaches working capital or how managing cash, receivables, stock and payables keeps it healthy; the nearest points cover financing and why small businesses fail, which are related but different ideas.

draft.title: Working capital management
card: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Current assets are things the business expects to turn into cash within a year, such as cash, receivables and stock. Current liabilities are debts due within a year, such as payables.
Receivables are amounts customers owe the business. Payables are amounts the business owes its suppliers. Stock is goods held for sale.
Managing working capital means managing each part. A business can collect receivables sooner, hold only the stock it needs, and use the time suppliers allow to pay its payables.
Too little working capital means a business may struggle to pay its bills on time. Too much means money is tied up in assets that earn little, such as idle cash or unsold stock.
draft.remember: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, and managing each part keeps it at a healthy level.

a.q: A business has current assets of $80,000 and current liabilities of $50,000. What is its working capital?
a.why: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, so $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000. Adding the two gives $130,000, which is the tempting mistake, but liabilities are subtracted.
a.clue: Subtract the debts due within a year from the assets.

b.q: Priya's hardware store in Bathurst has a large amount of money tied up in unsold stock, and its working capital is far above what it needs. Which action would best manage this?
opts: Hold less stock and use the freed cash for other needs
Buy more stock to get bulk prices from suppliers
Pay all suppliers immediately to reduce payables
Give customers longer to pay their accounts
b.why: Holding less stock releases cash that is tied up in unsold goods, which keeps working capital at a healthy level. Buying more stock would tie up even more cash. Paying suppliers at once and giving customers longer to pay would both drain cash rather than fix the excess stock.
b.clue: Which action turns idle stock back into usable cash?

b.best: Hold less stock and use the freed cash for other needs
